title: Characterization of microbial dark matter at scale with MetaSBT and taxonomy-aware Sequence Bloom Trees - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractAccurately characterizing metagenome-assembled genomes remains a substantial challenge due to the presence of sequencing errors, incomplete assembly and contamination. Here, we present MetaSBT, a tool for organizing, indexing and characterizing microbial reference genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes, demonstrated in this study using viruses. MetaSBT identifies clusters of genomes across all seven taxonomic levels using the Sequence Bloom Tree data structure, which relies on Bloom filters to index large amounts of genomes based on their k-mer composition. We built an initial set of databases composed of over 190,000 viral genomes from public sources, grouped into sequence-consistent clusters at different taxonomic levels. We defined over 40,000 candidate species, ~80% of which, to our knowledge, do not match viral species in reference databases to date. Furthermore, we showed that our databases are useful to existing quantitative metagenomic profilers to unlock the detection of unknown microbes and the estimation of their abundance in metagenomic samples. The open-source framework and databases are fully integrated into the Galaxy platform.

MainMicrobial genomics and metagenomics1, the study of genetic material recovered directly from environmental samples, have revolutionized our understanding of microbial diversity and function, enabling us to identify and characterize microbial species and communities without the need for cultivation2, with profound implications for a wide variety of scientific fields, including medicine, agriculture, environmental science and biotechnology. However, harnessing the full potential of large metagenomic datasets presents major computational and analytical challenges. Accurately identifying and characterizing the myriad microbes within complex environmental samples requires robust bioinformatics tools capable of handling massive datasets, resolving complex relationships between species and accounting for the vast unknown diversity that still eludes our current understanding. Although gold-standard taxonomies exist for prokaryotes (for example, GTDB3 and MGnify4) and viruses (ICTV5, vConTACT2 (ref. 6) and VIRIDIC7), current computational methods struggle to scale these taxonomies to the magnitude of current metagenomic output. One of the main challenges here is the clustering of genomes into taxonomically consistent groups. In this context, we adopt the American Society for Microbiology’s definition of microbes to include all microscopic life forms and viruses. Consequently, in this study, we refer to the vast uncharacterized fraction of both prokaryotic and viral entities with the term microbial dark matter.Traditionally, microbial genomes have been clustered using methods that consider their phylogeny, which infers the evolutionary relationships between organisms and defines huge phylogenetic trees8. These are built by aligning genomes of different organisms and identifying similarities among their genomic regions. However, phylogenetic methods are not well suited for clustering large datasets of genomes, mainly because requiring the alignment of all the genomes under study can be computationally prohibitive, especially for datasets containing hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of genomes.In recent years, several methods have been developed for the clustering of microbial genomes based on the analysis of k-mers, that is, by comparing the set of k-mers present in each genome in the dataset2,9. Genomes that share a large number of k-mers are likely more closely related than genomes that share a small number of k-mers. However, existing k-mer-based methods, such as the widely used species-level genome bins approach based on the average-linkage hierarchical clustering of microbial genomes2, rely on fixed thresholds to delineate clusters at different taxonomic levels (5% of genetic distance to define species, 10% to define genera and 30% to define families). This approach can limit the ability to capture finer-grained taxonomic distinctions, especially for less well-characterized microbial lineages, where the boundaries between clusters of genomes may be less clear, or for higher taxonomic levels, where thresholds cannot be easily defined. Additionally, the thresholds on the genomes’ genetic distances have been designed to work with Bacteria and Archaea and cannot be directly applied to other microbial kingdoms.Given these limitations, we built a framework to organize large amounts of microbial genomes. We leveraged Sequence Bloom Trees (SBTs)10, hierarchies of Bloom filters (BFs), probabilistic data structures that efficiently store k-mer presence information. Unlike traditional alignment, which scales quadratically, SBTs allow for rapid containment queries, enabling the interrogation of massive sequence collections with minimal memory footprint.MetaSBT is a scalable k-mer-based framework specifically designed for the incremental clustering of massive amounts of microbial reference genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), with the final aim of uncovering groups of yet-to-be-named microbes at different taxonomic levels.Here, we provide a detailed description of the MetaSBT framework, including its underlying methodology and data structures, with its software architecture illustrated in Fig. 1. We constructed and validated MetaSBT databases and applied the framework to a set of publicly available viral genomes for building a series of public MetaSBT databases. We exploited our databases to extend and improve the ability of quantitative taxonomic profilers to detect still-unknown viral species and integrate our framework and its databases into the Galaxy platform for broader accessibility.Fig. 1: The MetaSBT framework architecture is divided into three distinct but interconnected operational modules.Full size imageModule 1: index. Reference genomes and taxonomic metadata retrieved from public repositories (for example, NCBI GenBank) undergo quality assessment and dereplication. Next, optimal k-mer length and BF size are estimated. The core index is then constructed bottom–up, from the species level up to the kingdom level, producing a hierarchy of SBTs, which serves as the foundational MetaSBT reference database. Module 2: profile. Uncharacterized input genomes (for example, MAGs) are queried against the index. The framework performs a top–down database traversal (kingdom to species), using bitwise distance estimation to find the closest cluster match. This module outputs a full taxonomic classification label for the input sequence based on containment proximity. Module 3: update. To expand the database without requiring a computationally expensive from-scratch reconstruction, collections of uncharacterized genomes trigger an internal call to the profile module. The framework evaluates a decision node: is the genome within a known cluster boundary? If yes, the genome is assigned to the existing taxonomy, and that specific subtree is updated. If no, MetaSBT isolates the unassigned genomes and calculates intracluster distances to delineate structurally robust novel clusters. These new taxonomic topologies are dynamically integrated into the tree, resulting in an expanded, updated database that iteratively maps unknown microbial sequence space. DB, database.Although MetaSBT is a general-purpose framework applicable to all microbial domains, this study used the viral domain as the primary test environment to demonstrate the scalability and accuracy of the system under high-diversity conditions.ResultsWe built the first baseline of the database using all the viral reference genomes in NCBI GenBank11. The set of references comprised 26,285 genomes organized into 17 phyla, 38 classes, 63 orders, 161 families, 1,014 genera and 8,169 species. Genomes were automatically retrieved with the get_ncbi_genomes subroutine implemented in MetaSBT, which establishes whether a genome in NCBI GenBank is a reference genome or a MAG (or vMAG specifically, with ‘v’ standing for viral) according to a series of rules, as reported in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4.We also retrieved a set of 1,111 vMAGs from NCBI GenBank, where genomes are classified as vMAGs according to the same set of rules. We used these genomes to produce a database by updating the initial database with reference genomes only. The update process resulted in the definition of 28 unknown orders, as far as we know, 79 families, 268 genera and 936 species.To demonstrate the ability of MetaSBT to handle heterogeneous sources, we also considered the viral sequences distributed in the public Metagenomic Gut Virus (MGV) catalog12 over the MetaSBT database, with NCBI GenBank genomes and vMAGs as an incremental update. MGV contains a metagenomic compendium of roughly 190,000 DNA viruses from the human gut microbiome, which we treated as vMAGs for updating our database. It greatly expanded the set of unknown taxa to 2,976 additional classes, 6,460 orders, 8,622 families, 12,634 genera and 31,624 species. The MGV genomes were originally identified using a comprehensive viral detection pipeline developed by the MGV team, which integrates multiple features and classifiers to distinguish viral contigs from non-viral contigs in metagenomic assemblies. The pipeline combines gene prediction via Prodigal13, functional annotation through HMMER14 searches against both viral (Integrated Microbial Genomes/Virus Resource) and microbial (Pfam) marker gene databases15,16, k-mer-based viral sequence scoring using VirFinder17 and sequence-level characteristics such as strand switch rates. The final classification step is based on a rule-based system that integrates these features using logic that is adapted to different contig length ranges. This pipeline is well explained in the MGV publication12 and on GitHub at https://github.com/snayfach/MGV. We are currently planning to adopt the same procedure in future analyses of publicly available metagenomic samples. The viral genomes recovered from these samples will be periodically integrated into MetaSBT.The MetaSBT database presented here was constructed using the whole set of k-mers in the involved genomes. As previously explained, we used KITSUNE, which reported nine as the best k-mer size for our set of genomes. This parameter was also used to establish a proper BF size, which is determined using ntCard, defined as the total number of distinct k-mers. As detailed in the previous section, we applied our 100% over provisioning factor to the estimated BF size to accommodate future updates and avoid early saturation, and we used a single hash function to maximize index construction and query speed.Because the k-mer size is involved in every aspect of the MetaSBT framework, once established, it can only be changed at the price of rebuilding the whole database from scratch. This is why it is important to estimate a proper kingdom-specific k-mer size before building a database.Figure 2 shows the distribution of 40,729 MetaSBT clusters at the species level in descending order based on the number of genomes, comprising 8,169 known (~20%; red) and 32,560 unknown (~80%; black) species. We limited the number of clusters in the bar plot to species with more than 100 genomes (39 known and 207 unknown clusters), thus focusing on 0.6% of the clusters in our database. We also report a histogram in the top-right portion of the figure to show the number of known and unknown clusters, considering only species with equal to or less than 100 genomes (8,130 known and 32,353 unknown clusters), with the number of single-genome clusters equal to 25,579 (7,192 known and 18,387 unknown clusters).Fig. 2: Species-level distribution of known (red) and unknown (black) clusters across genomes and vMAGs.Full size imageClusters with more than 100 genomes (39 known and 207 unknown) are sorted in descending order based on their size, while the histogram reports the number of known and unknown clusters with equal to or less than 100 genomes, that is, 8,130 and 32,353, respectively.Analogously, considering a total of 13,916 genera, 1,014 were known (~7.3%), whereas 12,902 were, to our knowledge, unknown (~92.7%). At the family level, considering a total of 8,862 clusters, 161 were known (~1.9%), whereas 8,701 were unknown (~98.1%). The order level was instead composed of 6,551 clusters, of which 63 were known (~1%), whereas 6,488 were unknown (~99%). With 3,014 classes, only 38 clusters were known (~1.3%), whereas 2,976 were still unknown (~98.7%). Finally, all 17 phyla defined in MetaSBT were known.The complete list of known and unknown clusters across all seven taxonomic levels, detailing the number of reference genomes and vMAGs, BF density and mean completeness and contamination, can be accessed via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18).We adopted an inclusive indexing strategy regarding genomic quality. We consciously chose not to discard low-quality genomes during the indexing phase, as these often constitute the only available evidence of novel lineages in microbial dark matter. Prefiltering these genomes out would artificially reduce the diversity of the index and obscure potential discoveries.Although we did not apply prefiltering based on quality-control metrics, the complete list of viral genomes and sequences considered in our study, alongside their completeness and contamination scores computed by CheckV, is available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18). This approach shifts the decision-making power to the user, allowing for dynamic postquery filtering based on specific stringency requirements rather than limiting analyses to arbitrary inclusion thresholds.Additionally, to rigorously quantify our database and directly address potential overestimations caused by redundant assemblies, we performed a stringent post hoc dereplication at the species level. All genomes within each of the 40,729 species-level clusters were dereplicated at a 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI) threshold. During this process, reference genomes were prioritized as cluster representatives, and redundant sequences were collapsed. The complete dereplication mapping, which details the retained representatives, the discarded redundancies and their corresponding ANI distances, can be accessed via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18).Following dereplication, we sought to isolate a tier of high-confidence novel viral species. We established a strict recurrence threshold: an unknown cluster was marked as high confidence only if it maintained at least three distinct, nonredundant genomes after dereplication.Although the total number of genomes within these clusters was heavily reduced by the 99% ANI filter, with 79,450 redundant genomes (accounting for 36.6% of the initial assemblies) discarded during the process, the structural integrity of the clusters remained intact, leaving a highly confident core of 302 identified viral species, whose distribution is shown in Fig. 3.Fig. 3: Size distribution and taxonomic novelty of high-confidence unknown viral species after dereplication.Full size imageThe histogram illustrates the distribution of the identified 302 highly confident, identified viral species clusters. The height of each black bar represents the number of distinct, nonredundant genomes retained within the corresponding species-level cluster after applying a stringent 99% ANI dereplication filter. All depicted clusters satisfy our recurrence threshold of retaining at least three structurally distinct genomes after dereplication to confidently exclude potential assembly artifacts.Quantitatively, this high-confidence dark matter features contributions from several major viral lineages, revealing a striking divergence between cluster frequency and absolute genome volume. When evaluating the proportion of distinct species clusters (Fig. 3, Overall genus composition), Circovirus and Rotavirus were the most frequently assigned known genera, accounting for 17.2% and 8.9% of the 302 reported clusters, respectively. However, most of these clusters (69.9%) were grouped under Other Known Genera, representing a long tail of rare viral lineages. Conversely, when examining the absolute genomic volume (Fig. 3), that is, the total number of nonredundant genomes contributing to the unknown species space, Mimivirus completely dominated the dataset, comprising 7,911 genomes despite representing a smaller fraction of distinct clusters. Other major contributors by genomic volume include Carjivirus (971 genomes), Circovirus (598 genomes), Rotavirus (563 genomes) and Kingevirus (560 genomes).It is of note that MetaSBT databases are fully reproducible, and the pipeline used to generate them in an incremental way is available and documented on GitHub at the MetaSBT databases repository at https://github.com/cumbof/MetaSBT-DBs (ref. 19).Misclassification of genomes in NCBI GenBankAlthough NCBI GenBank serves as an invaluable cornerstone of genomic research, discrepancies between sequence-based clustering and historical taxonomy are inevitable due to evolving classification standards and the rapid growth of deposited data. We term these instances ‘taxonomic incongruences’: they often arise when legacy submissions rely on phenotypic criteria that differ from modern genomic standards (for example, ANI demarcation). Such inconsistencies can propagate into downstream analyses, potentially obscuring true biodiversity patterns. MetaSBT addresses this challenge by applying a consistent genomic comparison framework.First, we performed an average-linkage hierarchical clustering of all viral reference genomes retrieved from NCBI GenBank. Because we are dealing with BFs as sketch representations of genomes, we used the Jaccard index as a measure of genetic similarity. Considering two genomes A and B, the Jaccard index is defined as 1 minus the cardinality of the intersection over the cardinality of the union of A and B’s sets of unique k-mers, as reported in Eq. (1) below.$${J}_{k}(A,B)=1-\frac{\left|A\cap B\right|}{\left|A\cup B\right|}$$
(1)
We then estimated the ANI between A and B without the need for an exact alignment by applying the formula shown below (Eq. (2), where k is the k-mer size and Jk is the Jaccard index, as reported in Eq. (1))20,21,22,23:$${ANI}(A,B)=\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\times \mathrm{ln}\frac{2\times {J}_{k}(A,B)}{1+{J}_{k}(A,B)}\right)\times 100$$
(2)
Clusters were delineated by applying a threshold of 95% on the ANI, representing a 5% genetic-distance cutoff. This threshold was chosen to group genomes with a high degree of sequence similarity while allowing for natural genomic variation within taxonomic groups, and it was selected to align with the community standards for uncultivated viral genomes per the Minimum Information About an Uncultivated Virus Genome guidelines24.Each defined cluster was assigned a taxonomic label through a majority-voting mechanism. This involved considering the NCBI taxonomic labels of all genomes within a cluster and selecting the most frequent label as the representative taxonomy for the entire cluster. In cases where two or more clusters shared the same taxonomic label, we distinguished them as distinct clades by assigning them an incremental numerical ID.Among the set of 26,285 clustered reference genomes retrieved according to our previously described extended definition of reference, 686 genomes fell in clusters whose taxonomic label was different from the one reported in NCBI GenBank. Although MetaSBT does not use the taxonomic labels of vMAGs as reported in NCBI GenBank, it is worth noting that among the set of 1,111 vMAGs considered in the first update of the database, 1,051 genomes were misclassified in NCBI GenBank.It is also worth noting that applying the widely adopted threshold of 5% on the genetic distance for defining species during the generation of the first baseline of the MetaSBT database led to 530 species being redefined into a total of 3,236 clades, involving a total of 13,153 genomes. For instance, 2,456 genomes belonging to the Rotavirus A species were reorganized into 217 different clades.The list of misclassified genomes and the list of taxonomies affected by the de novo clustering of reference genomes are available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18).It is also relevant that, following the clustering, 191 taxonomies disappeared because their genomes fell into clusters with a different taxonomic label assigned through the majority-voting mechanism as previously mentioned.These findings are particularly relevant because there is a growing awareness of the importance of improving the classification of genomes in public databases, with different attempts to mitigate this problem proposed in the last few years25,26.Validation of BF-based ANI estimationTo validate the accuracy of the containment-based ANI estimation used by MetaSBT, we performed a direct correlation analysis against Mash, the current gold standard for alignment-free distance estimation. While Mash uses MinHash sketches to estimate the Jaccard index (J), MetaSBT approximates J using bitwise overlap of BFs. Establishing concordance between these methods is critical to ensure that MetaSBT’s taxonomic boundaries align with established genomic standards.We selected a random subset of 100 viral reference genomes and performed all-versus-all pairwise comparisons (N = 4,950 pairs). For each pair, we computed the ANI distance using two independent methods. For the first method, MetaSBT (BF), genomes were indexed using standard viral database parameters: k = 9 and a fixed BF size of m = 300,000 bits (using a single hash function, h = 1). The Jaccard index was derived from the bitwise containment of the filters. For the second method, Mash (MinHash), the same genomes were sketched using Mash with a sketch size of s = 1,000 and k = 9, and distances were computed using the standard Mash distance formula.We observed a strong linear correlation between the two estimation methods, with a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.9382. This high degree of statistical concordance confirms that MetaSBT’s BF-based approximation provides a highly reliable proxy for MinHash-based ANI, even with the probabilistic noise inherent to single-hash BFs. This strong concordance validates the use of our containment metric for defining robust taxonomic boundaries consistent with community standards.Computational scalability and comparative performanceWe benchmarked MetaSBT across its three core operations using subsets of increasing size (from a minimum of 1,000 up to 100,000 genomes) to assess computational efficiency. We show the computational scalability of MetaSBT across its three core operations using a resource trajectory plot, which simultaneously mapped wall-clock time (x axis) and peak memory footprint (y axis) on a logarithmic scale (Fig. 4).Fig. 4: Computational scalability and resource trajectories of MetaSBT core operations.Full size imageWall-clock time (x axis, hours) mapped against the peak memory footprint (y axis, GB) on a log–log scale for index construction (blue line), query profiling (green line) and batch updating (red line). Annotations indicate the number of genomes processed at each data point, scaling from 1,000 to 100,000 genomes. The straight trajectories across multiple orders of magnitude demonstrate strict linear scaling for both time and memory. Index construction was benchmarked up to the limit of the available viral reference dataset (25,000), while the profiling and update operations successfully scaled to 100,000 vMAGs.For the index construction phase (blue line), we benchmarked four database sizes (1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 25,000 genomes), representing the full scale of our available viral reference dataset (26,285 reference genomes). The straight trajectory indicates a strict linear scaling for both time and memory footprint. This predictable behavior is achieved because MetaSBT leverages existing taxonomic labels to structure the database, thereby avoiding the quadratic pairwise comparisons required by de novo clustering tools.Similarly, the query profiling phase (green line) benchmarked batch sizes ranging from 1,000 to 100,000 vMAGs against the reference-only version of our MetaSBT database. The linear trajectory confirms MetaSBT’s suitability for high-throughput screening applications. Whether analyzing a single isolate or a complex metagenomic dataset with thousands of contigs, the computational cost per query remains constant and predictable.Finally, the update phase (red line) measured the resources required to add batches of additional genomes (ranging from 1,000 to 100,000 vMAGs) to the pre-existing database. The trajectory scales strictly linearly with the size of the incoming batch. Additional viral genomes can be continuously integrated into the global index with a cost proportional only to the data size, eliminating the need for computationally expensive full-database reconstruction required by traditional methods.Furthermore, to evaluate the taxonomic resolution and scalability of MetaSBT, we performed a comparative benchmark against two state-of-the-art viral clustering tools: VIRIDIC7 (based on intergenomic distance estimation) and vConTACT2 (ref. 6; based on gene-sharing network). The benchmarking dataset was designed to simulate a realistic database-update scenario, comprising two distinct temporal snapshots of the NCBI GenBank viral assembly repository. The first snapshot, serving as the baseline dataset, represents the initial state of the database. It consists of the dataset used to construct the first reference-only version of the MetaSBT virus database, comprising all viral reference genomes available in NCBI GenBank as of April 2023 (approximately 26,000 genomes). The second snapshot is an additional dataset representing a batch update of recently sequenced genomes. It consists of a portion of the viral reference genomes deposited in NCBI GenBank between April 2023 and September 2025 that was not yet present in the MetaSBT database. These genomes were treated as vMAGs during the update process to simulate the real-world scenario of indexing novel, uncharacterized sequences. From the ~200,000 entries available in this period, we downsampled to ~6,000 genomes by retaining only one representative genome per identified species to create a balanced query set.Although MetaSBT is engineered for linear scalability, traditional alignment-based approaches face major computational hurdles when scaling to tens of thousands of genomes. Specifically, VIRIDIC exhibits quadratic scaling due to its reliance on exhaustive pairwise intergenomic distance calculations. Consequently, executing VIRIDIC on the full experimental dataset of ~32,000 genomes (~26,000 baseline and ~6,000 additional genomes) was computationally prohibitive, as it would necessitate nearly 1 billion pairwise alignments. Similarly, although vConTACT2 uses optimal protein alignment (DIAMOND27), clustering massive networks of this scale can become resource-intensive compared to alignment-free methods, particularly in terms of memory usage for network graph construction.To enable a valid comparison without compromising taxonomic complexity, we used a vertical-slice subsampling strategy. Rather than selecting a random subset of individual genomes, which would artificially fragment taxonomic groups, we randomly selected entire taxonomic lineages (genera). For 20 randomly selected genera, we extracted all associated genomes from both the baseline and additional datasets. This approach reduced the total input size to 2,000 genomes (1,617 from the baseline dataset and the remaining 383 from the additional dataset) while preserving the full evolutionary context and intragenus diversity required for accurate clustering.The three tools were executed using the following configurations to ensure comparable operational conditions on the benchmark subset of 2,000 viral genomes. First, MetaSBT was assessed on its ability to correctly update an existing taxonomy, as well as identify and establish taxonomic groups for unclassified sequences. This involved a two-step workflow: an initial indexing phase where a database was constructed using only the baseline subset of genomes (k = 9 and a BF size estimated automatically via ntCard), followed by a profiling and update phase in which the additional subset of genomes was queried against the index, assigning genomes to their corresponding baseline clusters or establishing new clusters when appropriate.Second, VIRIDIC v1.1 was executed on the combined dataset (baseline and additional datasets) to generate a ground-truth ANI clustering. During processing, default intergenomic similarity thresholds were applied (species: 95% ANI; genus: 70% ANI). Additionally, to accommodate the serialization of large intergenomic distance matrices generated by the all-versus-all alignment, the R environment’s global size limit was adjusted to a minimum of 25 gigabytes (GB).Finally, vConTACT2 v0.11.3 was executed on the combined dataset to assess clustering based on shared protein content. For input processing, nucleotide sequences from the combined dataset were first converted to amino acid sequences using Prodigal13 v2.6.3 in metagenomic mode to ensure consistent gene prediction across all fragments. The resulting protein sequences were supplied to vConTACT2, where DIAMOND was used for sensitive protein–protein alignment and the Markov clustering algorithm was selected to partition the gene-sharing network. To prevent bias from external reference databases, the tool was run in de novo mode, ensuring that the resulting clustering was driven exclusively by the input sequences.vConTACT2 produced the fewest clusters (133) with the largest average size (14.88 genomes per cluster) and the lowest singleton rate (22.6%). This reflects a broad-spectrum aggregation strategy, grouping genomes into wide taxonomic units based on shared proteins.By contrast, VIRIDIC produced the highest number of clusters (1,605) with the highest singleton rate (91.2%). This indicates that applying strict alignment-based ANI thresholds (95%) often results in fine-scale fragmentation, where many genomes fail to group with others due to alignment gaps or high sequence divergence.Finally, MetaSBT produced an intermediate number of clusters (723) with a lower singleton rate (86.4%) than VIRIDIC. This demonstrates that MetaSBT operates at a high-resolution species level (similar to VIRIDIC) but is more robust in grouping divergent genomes. The k-mer containment approach identified relationships that strict alignment missed, bridging the gap between the hyperfragmentation of VIRIDIC and the broad aggregation of vConTACT2.Clustering concordance was quantified using the adjusted rand index (ARI), V-measure, homogeneity and completeness to assess the similarity between the ground-truth clusters (as defined by VIRIDIC and vConTACT2) and the MetaSBT assignments. To ensure computational feasibility for the alignment-based tools while preserving full taxonomic context, this benchmark was performed on a vertical slice of 2,000 viral genomes representing 20 randomly selected genera.The ARI serves as a strict measure of one-to-one cluster correspondence. ARI penalizes both splitting (one true cluster becomes two predicted clusters) and merging (two true clusters become one) equally. The V-measure, defined as the harmonic mean of homogeneity (clusters contain only members of a single class) and completeness (all members of a class are assigned to the same cluster), is particularly sensitive to hierarchical consistency; a high score indicates that the clusters of one method map cleanly into the clusters of the other, even if the resolution (granularity) differs. Furthermore, homogeneity, also known as purity, measures whether each predicted cluster contains only members of a single class, with a score of 1.0 indicating perfectly pure clusters (no mixing of different reference taxa within a single cluster). Finally, completeness measures whether all members of a given class are assigned to the same cluster, where a score of 1.0 indicates that reference taxa are not split across multiple clusters.When comparing MetaSBT with the alignment-based VIRIDIC, the framework achieved a high V-measure (0.7708) and completeness (0.9970), with a homogeneity score of 0.6282 and an ARI of 0.0922. Against the protein-sharing network of vConTACT2, MetaSBT yielded a higher ARI (0.3547) and homogeneity (0.7907), with robust V-measure (0.7472) and completeness (0.7083) scores. To establish a baseline of agreement between the established tools, VIRIDIC and vConTACT2 were compared with each other, resulting in an ARI of 0.2419, a V-measure of 0.7196, homogeneity of 0.5630 and completeness of 0.9970.Regarding the comparison between MetaSBT and VIRIDIC, the divergence between the low ARI (0.09) and high V-measure (0.77) is a marker of resolution mismatch rather than classification error. This pattern indicates that MetaSBT acts as a high-resolution discriminator, enforcing strict species boundaries based on k-mer containment, whereas VIRIDIC’s default clustering often aggregates these groups into coarser, broader taxonomic units. Crucially, the high V-measure confirms that MetaSBT’s assignments are hierarchically consistent; the finer-grained clusters produced by MetaSBT are pure subsets of the broader VIRIDIC groups. This demonstrates that MetaSBT accurately captures the underlying sequence relationships but enforces sequence boundaries more strictly than the alignment-based heuristic.By contrast, the comparison between MetaSBT and vConTACT2 yielded a higher ARI (0.35) and a similar robust V-measure (0.75). The higher ARI suggests that MetaSBT’s k-mer-based boundaries align more closely with protein-network boundaries than with pure ANI thresholds in certain contexts. However, the imperfect ARI is expected and biologically justifiable: vConTACT2 clusters based on gene content and shared protein families, which evolve at a different rate than the whole-genome nucleotide sequences used by MetaSBT. The strong V-measure again confirms that MetaSBT’s taxonomy is biologically congruent with the protein-network topology. MetaSBT groups are not randomly distributed across the network but represent cohesive submodules within the larger viral clusters defined by vConTACT2.Finally, to contextualize MetaSBT’s performance, we compared the two gold standards against each other. Notably, the concordance between VIRIDIC and vConTACT2 (ARI = 0.24, V-measure = 0.72) is lower than the concordance between MetaSBT and vConTACT2. This result is critical and demonstrates that there is no single ground truth in viral taxonomy. Even established tools using different biological signals (nucleotide ANI versus protein conservation) disagree considerably on cluster boundaries.MetaSBT’s performance must be interpreted relative to this baseline variation. Its V-measure scores against both tools (>0.74) exceed the agreement found between the two control methods (0.72). This indicates that MetaSBT provides a taxonomic organization that is as consistent with established biological signals as the current state-of-the-art tools are with each other, while offering unique advantages in terms of scalability for massive datasets.Unlocking the quantitative profiling of unknown microbes in metagenomic samples with Kraken2+BrackenAccurately characterizing the composition of microbial communities in metagenomic samples relies on our ability to identify and quantify the presence of both known and, crucially, unknown microbes. Traditional methods often struggle with the latter, but the integration of MetaSBT databases with Kraken2 (ref. 28) offers a powerful solution to rapidly detect unknown taxa in metagenomic samples.Kraken2 is a quantitative taxonomic classification tool that uses exact k-mer matching to rapidly and accurately assign taxonomic labels to metagenomic sequences. The process begins with the construction of a Kraken2 database from a set of genomes, representing known (and, in our case, unknown) microbial taxa. The database stores all possible k-mers found within these genomes, along with their associated taxonomic information. When presented with a metagenomic sample for classification, Kraken2 fragments the reads into their constituent k-mers and queries the database to identify which taxa are most likely to contain those specific k-mers. To make the final assignment, Kraken2 uses a lowest common ancestor algorithm. If a read’s k-mers match multiple taxa within the database, Kraken2 assigns it to the lowest taxonomic rank shared by all matches. This approach helps account for uncertainties arising from shared genomic regions or incomplete database representation.Using Kraken2 for benchmarking our databases comes with a series of advantages in terms of speed with extremely fast classifications and flexibility of its databases that can be fully customized, including taxa as defined by MetaSBT.Specifically, we used the taxonomic organization of all the 217,041 viral genomes in our MetaSBT database to build a custom Kraken2 database by running the kraken subroutine provided with MetaSBT, which requires only 1.2 GB of storage space.To benchmark the performance of our custom Kraken2 database, we focused on publicly available metagenomic samples from a study that investigated gut microbiome composition and metabolic activity in the context of Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis and non-inflammatory bowel disease controls across a US and Dutch cohort29. First, we did not dereplicate genomes, especially vMAGs, to allow unknown clusters to grow over time with subsequent incremental updates and potentially confirm those growing clusters as actual novel taxa. This eventually allows us to discriminate actual taxa from artifacts (see dedicated section below). Second, we considered all reference genomes and vMAGs regardless of their quality to eventually allow users to identify junk sequences among their set of input sequences.The emergence of clusters populated by vMAGs and not assigned to any known species within the database presents both exciting opportunities and interpretative challenges. Although such clusters may represent actual novel taxa, it is essential to approach their interpretation with caution.Several factors can contribute to the formation of clusters that do not necessarily represent distinct species. First, because vMAGs are inherently incomplete representations of genomes, clustering based on this partial data can lead to the artificial separation of closely related species; thus, the adoption of proper techniques for assessing the quality of such genomes is highly encouraged, as described earlier. Additionally, microbial genome plasticity and horizontal gene transfer can confound phylogenetic analyses, meaning that clusters may emerge from the acquisition or loss of specific genomic regions rather than representing true species boundaries. Finally, the resolution of any taxonomic classification method is inherently limited by the comprehensiveness and potential biases of the underlying database. Consequently, clusters composed of vMAGs that are absent from reference databases might simply reflect gaps in our current knowledge rather than genuinely novel species.Therefore, it is crucial to avoid prematurely assigning species-level classifications to clusters solely based on their initial formation. Longitudinal analysis, incorporating database updates and the addition of vMAGs, can provide valuable insights into the validity of clusters through several key indicators. First, regarding cluster stability, clusters that consistently expand with additional data while demonstrating internal coherence and distinct boundaries from other clusters are more likely to represent genuine taxonomic groups. Second, cluster quality, specifically the completeness and contamination of its genomes, should also be taken into account when discriminating real clusters from potential artifacts. Finally, through comparative genomics, in-depth analyses of vMAGs within a cluster focusing on core gene content, ANI and functional potential can provide further evidence against their classification as a novel species.Among the 246 species with more than 100 genomes (Fig. 2), 207 were still unknown, with numbers of vMAGs ranging from 101 to 1,834 for the smallest and the largest unknown species, respectively. Additionally, 32 of these 207 unknown species were high-quality clusters (that is, on average, the completeness and contamination of the genomes in these clusters were >90% and ≤5%, respectively), while 174 of them were medium quality (that is, completeness of ≥50% and contamination of ≤10%), and the remaining 1 cluster was low quality (that is, completeness of <50% and contamination of ≤10%).Conversely, most species defined by MetaSBT with less than or equal to 100 genomes were still unknown. Among them, of the 32,353 clusters, 13,966 unknown species contained more than a single genome, with 3,727 high-quality, 9,811 medium-quality and 428 low-quality clusters, according to the same thresholds of completeness and contamination defined above.The identification of unknown clusters raises the fundamental question of distinguishing true biological novelty from assembly artifacts. Rather than viewing this ambiguity as a limitation, we propose the cluster-stability hypothesis as a validation heuristic inherent to incremental frameworks. We posit that the biological validity of a cluster is reflected in its growth trajectory over time. A cluster that represents a genuine biological taxon will likely recruit additional members as diverse metagenomic datasets are indexed. By contrast, clusters that remain static (that is, cardinality remains constant) despite the addition of thousands of genomes are more likely to represent sequencing errors, chimeras or rare artifacts. Furthermore, the use of SBTs ensures that this unknown status implies considerable evolutionary divergence. Due to the containment property of SBTs, incomplete fragments of known viruses would still be classified within known clusters. Thus, the stable growth of these unknown groups strongly suggests the discovery of cohesive, previously uncharacterized viral lineages.Additionally, as reported in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18), it is worth noting that 46,649 vMAGs (that is, ~19% of all processed vMAGs) among those retrieved from NCBI GenBank and MGV did not match any of the clusters defined in MetaSBT (marked as Unassigned), not even at the kingdom level. Because the characterization of genomes in MetaSBT relies on cluster boundaries and thus on the set of k-mers of all genomes in the database, it does not necessarily mean that these genomes are not viruses. The root node of the database tree contains the whole genetic content in terms of k-mers of all genomes in the database. The set of k-mers of these unassigned and still uncharacterized genomes is not close enough to anything seen so far, and thus they must be reconsidered for future updates. We are fully committed to expanding the virus database by integrating additional publicly available datasets of genomes and sequences, and by eventually assembling genomes from public metagenomes. We also plan to release other MetaSBT databases focused on different microbial kingdoms, including Bacteria, Archaea and Fungi. Additionally, future software versions will enable the use of average amino acid identity in conjunction with ANI. This will allow for more accurate clustering of genomes at higher taxonomic levels34.Although the empirical validation in this study focuses extensively on viruses, MetaSBT’s architecture is domain agnostic. In fact, from an algorithmic perspective, viral taxonomy presents a much more rigorous stress test for our taxonomic tree-of-trees architecture than bacterial or archaeal domains. Due to extreme sequence divergence across viral families, the lack of universal marker genes and highly fragmented taxonomies, viruses force MetaSBT to manage a much wider, disjointed tree topology. Bacteria, being more highly conserved by comparison, yield higher intra-species k-mer redundancies and more compact taxonomic paths. Furthermore, the underlying SBT data structure powering MetaSBT has already been exhaustively benchmarked on massive sequence datasets in its foundational publications, confirming that the core bitwise operations scale seamlessly to large inputs.To contextualize MetaSBT’s scalability for larger microbial kingdoms, we can estimate the footprint of a comprehensive bacterial index. Although an average bacterial genome is approximately 100 times larger than a viral genome, high intraspecies k-mer redundancy considerably compresses the required bit space in a BF environment. Extrapolating from the distinct k-mer cardinalities reported in massive bacterial indexing projects, such as BIGSI35 or Mantis36, which successfully indexed hundreds of thousands of microbial genomes, we estimate that a MetaSBT index for 100,000 bacterial genomes would require approximately 150–200 GB of disk space. This estimate should be validated empirically in future bacterial-scale benchmarks. Crucially, the RAM requirement is governed by the actively loaded paths rather than the full disk-resident index, keeping peak memory bounded and substantially lower than the total index footprint.Building and maintaining these comprehensive databases presents major challenges, particularly regarding the storage space required to track all the BFs within the database tree, whose inherent redundancy, by definition of an SBT, facilitates rapid and efficient search queries. The integration of MetaSBT and its databases into the Galaxy platform helps address these challenges through the availability of scalable storage and computational resources for building and updating the databases and for profiling genomes.Furthermore, Galaxy’s collaborative features streamline the sharing of MetaSBT data. Researchers can easily grant collaborators access to private MetaSBT databases by simply sharing their Galaxy history, without leaving the platform. The integration of the MetaSBT tool suite into Galaxy workflows opens exciting possibilities for streamlining metagenomic analyses, such as the workflows that already include the assembly of genomes from metagenomes. Its integration would allow the automatic, incremental expansion of MetaSBT databases with additional assembled genomes, enabling the detection of novel species and strains. Such a capability would be particularly valuable in clinical settings or research focused on studying the microbial composition of samples related to specific diseases and health conditions, where identifying previously uncharacterized microbes could also lead to the definition of specific biomarkers and eventually the development of personalized therapies.Moreover, the MetaSBT databases provide a powerful foundation for building custom databases for quantitative profilers such as Kraken2. This opens exciting scenarios, such as reanalyzing large-scale metagenomic studies related to different diseases and health conditions that could lead to uncovering previously undetected microbial biomarkers among still-unknown and yet-to-be-named species.Although the integration of MetaSBT databases with quantitative profilers successfully unlocked the detection of previously unknown viral lineages in a real-world clinical cohort, the differential abundance of these species did not directly correlate with the primary phenotypic structure of the samples. The distinct sample clustering observed in our analysis is likely driven by hidden variables or unrecorded clinical metadata rather than the primary inflammatory bowel disease diagnosis. Consequently, the immediate clinical impact of these specific viral lineages remains unclear. However, the results underscore the broader methodological contribution of the MetaSBT framework. By enabling the systematic indexing and quantification of microbial dark matter, it provides the necessary computational foundation for future large-scale association studies to routinely investigate unknown sequence space, representing a critical prerequisite for the discovery of microbial biomarkers.In conclusion, MetaSBT provides a powerful and scalable framework for characterizing microbial diversity, enabling the discovery and analysis of novel taxa, and ultimately advancing our understanding of the microbial world.MethodsThe MetaSBT framework was entirely implemented in Python 3.8, leveraging HowDeSBT37, a software for building SBTs10,37,38, and extending its functionalities. SBTs are tree-like data structures whose nodes are BFs, probabilistic data structures used to represent sets, representing one of the most efficient ways to index massive amounts of data to date39. SBTs were designed specifically for indexing experimental sequence data, and BFs are usually built over sets of k-mers. In our case, we adopted this technology to index genomes. However, although HowDeSBT is quite fast and memory efficient, it comes with a limitation. Its unique way of encoding and clustering data, based on the concept of determined/how split filters37, does not allow it to incrementally update the tree with additional data once the tree is built, leaving the only option to rebuild the whole tree from scratch by extending the initial set of data (that is, genomes in our case). Providing the ability to update the tree without affecting the efficient way it clusters data is a must-have feature, because rebuilding everything from scratch every time we need to include a genome in the database is clearly not feasible, especially when dealing with thousands of genomes that require a substantial amount of computational resources to process.To overcome this issue, we propose taking advantage of the natural taxonomic classification of reference genomes from isolate sequencing. These are well known and fully classified, from the kingdom level all the way down to the species level. We used this information to build a series of SBTs, one for each taxonomic entity across all seven taxonomic levels (that is, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species), as described in the next section.MetaSBT comprises the following modules: (1) The index module, responsible for indexing a set of reference genomes, often retrieved from NCBI GenBank, by organizing them based on their taxonomic classification and building a series of SBTs at all taxonomic levels (Fig. 1, Module 1). It also supports a quality-control step and a dereplication procedure to exclude low-quality genomes and avoid processing the same genomes twice. (2) The profile module, responsible for the characterization of input genomes at all taxonomic levels by querying the database and reporting the distance between the input genome and the closest clusters (Fig. 1, Module 2). (3) The update module, responsible for updating the database with additional genomes. First, MetaSBT makes use of the profile module to establish the closest kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species and genome in the database from the input genomes. It then evaluates a critical decision node: whether the input genome falls within the ANI boundaries of the closest cluster. If it does, the genome is assigned to the existing taxonomy, and that specific subtree is efficiently updated. If it falls outside the closest cluster’s boundaries, the module isolates the unassigned genomes, calculates intracluster distances to delineate novel clusters and dynamically integrates these taxonomic topologies into the global database tree (Fig. 1, Module 3). The framework architecture is reported in Fig. 1.Exploiting the natural taxonomic classification of reference genomes to efficiently update an SBT-based databaseHere, we propose a way to decompose the SBT data structure into a series of SBTs, exploiting the taxonomic organization of reference genomes. This process starts by grouping genomes belonging to the same species and producing an SBT over their set of k-mers. This produces a tree for each species involved in the initial set of genomes. The root nodes of the species trees are then used as leaves for building the SBTs at the genus level, by grouping species belonging to the same genus according to their taxonomic classification. We grouped the root nodes of the species SBTs, which contained the entire genetic content of all the genomes under those specific trees. Thus, considering the root nodes is equivalent to analyzing the whole set of genomes used to build the species trees. The process continues iteratively by considering the root nodes of the genera trees as leaves for building the SBTs at the family level, and analogously for the order, class, phylum and, finally, kingdom level composed of a single SBT whose root node contains the genetic content of all genomes in the initial set of genomes. Adopting this technique updates the tree as follows: given a genome and once the closest genome in the database has been established, we should first determine whether the closest cluster (that is, the species to which the closest genome belongs) is close enough to eventually add the input genome to it, as shown in the next section.Here, we consider two options. First, if the input genome is found to be close enough to the closest species, we reconsider the whole set of genomes belonging to that species, plus the input genome, to rebuild the cluster at the species level. We then reconsider the root nodes of all clusters belonging to that specific genus to rebuild the genus tree and so on, repeating the same steps used to initially build the database. The difference here is that we rebuild a series of SBTs, one for each of the seven taxonomic levels, corresponding to a single branch of the whole SBT database. Alternatively, if we determine that the input genome is not close enough to the closest species in the database, we can then define a species, as soon as the input genome is found to be close enough to the closest genus tree, and so on. This results in defining clusters at different taxonomic levels that, in case of updating the database with MAGs, do not contain any reference genomes at all, representing still-unknown species. This process is described in depth in the next sections.Database size is directly proportional to BF lengthSBTs are tree-like data structures whose nodes are BFs, that is, probabilistic data structures used to represent sets. In our specific case, BFs are used to represent the set of distinct k-mers in a particular genome. The cardinality of k-mers also determines the size of the BFs, usually represented as bit vectors, where 1 denotes the presence of a specific k-mer and 0 represents its absence. k-Mers are indeed encoded as 1 at specific positions in the BF vectors that are established as the result of one or more hash functions applied on each k-mer.Establishing a proper BF size is a key aspect of defining the whole SBT database. The larger the BFs, the more storage space is required to maintain these data structures and the whole database, but smaller BFs translate into high false-positive rates, affecting their lookup capabilities. Thus, to estimate a proper BF size and also minimize their memory footprint, we propose estimating the optimal BF size for each taxonomic level, based on the total number of k-mers belonging to all the genomes under that specific level. Using a universal size for all the BFs in the database would produce sparse BFs, especially at the lower end of the taxonomic organization, potentially leading to a considerable waste of storage space.Instead, we estimate the BF size at the species level by summing the number of distinct k-mers from all the genomes belonging to each species. At the genus level, we estimate the BF size by summing the number of distinct k-mers from all the species belonging to each genus. This process is repeated iteratively up to the kingdom level, where the whole set of genomes in the database is considered to establish the BF size.This way, we define a different BF size for each taxonomic level, accounting for the different number of k-mers that is stored at each level. Depending on the number of genomes initially considered to build the database, this technique drastically reduces the storage space required to maintain the whole database tree.It is worth noting that the number of distinct k-mers strictly depends on their length. A larger k-mer size might also lead to larger BFs, impacting the storage requirements, as previously mentioned, in addition to the time required to query the data structures. Therefore, selecting an appropriate k-mer length is also crucial for balancing database size and performance. To address this, MetaSBT integrates KITSUNE40, a Python tool that enables the automatic estimation of an empirically optimal k-mer size based on a combination of the cumulative relative entropy, average number of common features and observed common features measures, computed on the initial set of genomes across a specific range of k-mer sizes.However, it is worth noting that the strategy mentioned above has the side effect of a faster saturation of the BFs at lower taxonomic levels. Although deciding whether to apply this procedure is a crucial first step in building a database, we can also mitigate the side effects, as described next.BF configuration and ntCard parametrizationA critical aspect of MetaSBT’s performance and efficiency lies in the configuration of the SBTs. To establish the optimal BF size, we perform an initial cardinality estimation of the total number of unique k-mers in the union of the initial set of reference genomes using ntCard41. Although singleton k-mers (those occurring only once) are excluded during this initial ntCard estimation to prevent sequencing errors from artificially inflating the baseline memory requirements, all k-mers (including singletons) are actively retained and inserted during the actual indexing phase. This ensures maximum sensitivity for low-abundance lineages and strain-level differentiation.Because MetaSBT is an incrementally updatable framework, we must prevent early saturation of the BFs as additional genomes are added over time. BF saturation typically occurs when the fill ratio exceeds 0.5 (that is, more than 50% of the bits are set to 1), at which point the false-positive rate (FPR) increases unacceptably and impacts the accuracy of the Jaccard distance approximation. To proactively avoid this, we implement an over-provisioning strategy: the base BF size estimated by ntCard is incremented by a 100% buffer before initialization. This doubling of capacity ensures that the filters can accommodate hundreds of thousands of genomes without requiring a computationally expensive database rebuild.Furthermore, MetaSBT is configured to use a single hash function per BF to maximize reconstruction and bitwise query speeds. Although using a single hash function yields a higher theoretical per-k-mer FPR than multiple hashes, the sequence-level FPR remains negligible. Because MetaSBT’s taxonomic assignment relies on the aggregate containment signal of thousands of k-mers (where the bitset essentially acts as a genomic fingerprint analogous to MinHash), isolated k-mer collisions do not considerably bias the overall Jaccard distance estimation or the downstream clustering.It is important to emphasize that this negligible impact on accuracy holds specifically because MetaSBT is designed to organize and query complete genome assemblies and genomes assembled from metagenomes, rather than individual short sequencing reads. Although a single hash function might introduce unacceptable noise for short-read classification (where a sequence may only contain a few dozen k-mers), at the scale of a genome, a massive aggregate signal easily overcomes the theoretical FPR.Crucially, the use of a single hash function is the mathematical mechanism that allows the bitwise comparison of BFs to accurately approximate the true k-mer Jaccard similarity. With h = 1, the BF effectively acts as a deterministic fingerprint of the input k-mer spectrum, where the activated slots directly represent the specific k-mer composition. If multiple hash functions were used, a single k-mer would map to multiple, overlapping bits. This would break the direct fingerprint relationship, making the bitwise intersection and union operations mathematically unrepresentative of the true Jaccard similarity.How close is close enough? Defining dynamic cluster boundariesTo profile a genome and eventually update a database, we should determine whether the input genome is close enough to its closest cluster at the species level in the database to be characterized as that specific species. To do so, we introduce the concept of cluster boundaries, defined as the minimum and maximum ANI distance between all genomes under a particular cluster. These numbers are computed for all the clusters at all seven taxonomic levels and give us an idea of the overall genetic diversity between genomes in the database. At the time of deciding whether a genome must be added to the closest cluster, we compare the ANI computed between the genome and closest cluster, and we finally compare it with the closest cluster’s boundaries. This eventually results in rebuilding the cluster or defining a new one, as mentioned earlier.To define the cluster boundaries, the cluster must contain at least three genomes. Thus, if a cluster contains less than three genomes, we implicitly estimate its boundaries as the average minimum and maximum of all the other clusters under the same upper taxonomic level. This is, however, only an approximation and a temporary solution, and the boundaries of these clusters must be recomputed with future incremental updates, as soon as they contain at least three genomes. At that point, all the MAGs previously assigned to that cluster that now fall outside those boundaries must be reprocessed and reclustered, eventually leading to the generation of clusters, as discussed below.A tree structure to speed up the characterization of genomesOnce we build an initial database with reference genomes only and compute the clusters’ boundaries, we are already able to profile genomes, which is also a step required to update the database. The first baseline must contain reference genomes only, because we use their taxonomic classification to define clusters across all seven taxonomic levels.To profile a genome, we exploit the tree structure to initially query the root node of the kingdom tree with the set of k-mers in the input genome. The query reports the number of k-mers in common between the input genome and kingdom. This process is repeated another six times by querying the root nodes of all the other clusters at the remaining taxonomic levels, up to the species level. Before querying a specific cluster and moving to the next taxonomic level, we first prune the database tree by considering a subset of clusters selected by applying a distance threshold based on the number of k-mers matching the closest cluster plus 25% of its value. Expanding the set of closest genomes by 25% in genetic distance can result in querying far more branches of the database tree, thus taking more time to establish the closest nodes, but it is also crucial for mitigating, and sometimes preventing, misclassifications due to horizontal gene transfer between distantly related species (for example, in human-associated microorganisms)42.After reaching the species level, we finally profile the input genome with the same taxonomy as the closest species, only if the ANI between the input genome and the closest species falls within that species’ boundaries. This process also reports the closest genome under the selected closest species, which is also the closest strain.Beyond known taxonomies: MetaSBT’s approach to defining microbial taxaAlthough established taxonomic classifications provide a valuable framework for understanding microbial diversity, they are inherently limited by current knowledge. Metagenomic studies constantly reveal novel microbial lineages that defy easy categorization within existing taxonomic ranks. This section explores how MetaSBT goes beyond known taxonomies, using a clustering-based approach to identify and define microbial taxa.To achieve this goal, MetaSBT starts from a baseline of known microbial reference genomes, that is, genomes from isolate sequencing characterized across all seven taxonomic levels, from the kingdom down to the species level. As previously discussed, MetaSBT exploits natural taxonomic classification to build a multitude of SBTs across all seven known taxonomic levels, producing the first baseline of the MetaSBT database. Cluster boundaries are then computed to provide users with an initial overview of the intracluster genetic diversity. These are also crucial for establishing, in conjunction with the profiles described earlier, whether a MAG should be assigned to the closest cluster or not.Starting from the species level, to assign a MAG to its closest species according to its profiles, MetaSBT does not directly look at the ANI between the input genome and the closest genome in the database. This is because the closest genome could be closer to the boundaries of its own cluster than other genomes in the same species. Thus, MetaSBT proceeds by computing the ANI between the input genome and centroid of the closest species (which could eventually overlap with the closest genome), defined as the genome that maximizes the ANI similarity with all other genomes in the same cluster. This is finally compared with the species boundaries to eventually assign the genome to that particular species.This process runs iteratively across all input genomes by keeping apart those that do not fall within the boundaries of any clusters at the species level in the database. If the process assigns a genome to its closest species, it then immediately performs an average-linkage hierarchical clustering on the pair-wise ANI matrix computed across all input genomes, finally using the boundary of the closest species as the threshold for identifying other genomes to be assigned to the same species.The same procedure is applied downward from the species level up to the kingdom level, using different thresholds based on the actual boundaries of the input genomes’ closest clusters. It is of note that no additional clusters have been created, and all input genomes have been assigned to a lineage with different levels of taxonomic novelty.To complete the definition of the assigned taxonomies, MetaSBT starts processing the input genomes by grouping them according to their partial common labels, from the kingdom level to the species level. Because these genomes did not fall within the boundaries of any clusters under this specific taxonomic level, MetaSBT estimates the boundaries of the clusters as the average between the boundaries of all the other clusters at the same taxonomic level. The estimated boundary is used as the threshold for defining clusters after the computation of average-linkage hierarchical clustering on the partially characterized genomes with the same common partial taxonomic label. The same process is repeated multiple times until a complete characterization of all the input genomes with at least one level of taxonomic novelty.This process results in the definition of clusters at different taxonomic levels that, by definition, do not contain any reference genomes at all, thus representing still unknown microbial characterizations.It is worth noting that, in the case of additional reference genomes, we do not rely solely on their already known taxonomy. We instead apply the same process performed on MAGs, but at the time of assigning references to already defined clusters in the database, their taxonomies contribute to the definition of the taxonomic characterization of the assigned clusters. In case the assigned cluster is unknown, it inherits the taxonomic profile of the references, thus losing its unknown traits. Otherwise, the taxonomic labels of the reference genomes, together with taxonomies of all the other references in the same assigned cluster, contribute to the majority-voting mechanism used to determine the most occurring taxonomy to characterize the cluster.Database integrity: quality control and dereplicationAs the database grows with additional genomes, we need to ensure its integrity by performing quality control and dereplication on the incoming genomes before adding them to the database.Quality control of input genomes is a necessary step to validate the completeness and contamination of genomes. MetaSBT integrates different quality-control frameworks to assess genome quality depending on their kingdom. More specifically, it integrates CheckV43 for viral genomes, CheckM44 for bacterial and archaeal genomes and BUSCO45 for eukaryotic genomes.MetaSBT also provides a dereplication procedure to ensure that no duplicate genomes are processed and included twice in the database. We set a dereplication threshold of 99% similarity between genomes by default based on their ANI distance.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability

Public databases are hosted on the Galaxy CVMFS33, and their metadata are also accessible through GitHub in the MetaSBT-DBs repository at https://github.com/cumbof/MetaSBT-DBs ref. 19, alongside the pipeline used to generate the databases in an incremental way. The custom Kraken and Bracken databases are also available in the same GitHub repository. Public databases are also indexed in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18).
Additionally, viral reference genomes and vMAGs used for building the first two versions of the MetaSBT virus databases are available on the NCBI GenBank repository (assembly summary report dated June 2024) at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank, while vMAGs used for building the third incremental update of the MetaSBT virus database are available on the MGV repository (v1.0 dated 8 July 2021) at https://portal.nersc.gov/MGV.
The comprehensive datasets supporting the findings of this study are openly available in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19892486 (ref. 18). This deposit includes a detailed summary of all MetaSBT clusters across all seven taxonomic levels, reporting assigned taxonomic labels, genome counts, BF densities and taxonomic novelty status. The repository also provides the complete CheckV quality-control statistics for all evaluated genomes, alongside the full species-level dereplication mapping at a 99% ANI threshold. This dereplication mapping details the retained structurally distinct cluster representatives, the discarded redundancies and the corresponding ANI distances justifying the dereplication.
Gut microbiome samples analyzed here in the context of Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis and non-inflammatory bowel disease control are publicly available on NCBI under BioProject number PRJNA400072.
Code availability

MetaSBT’s code is open source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/cumbof/MetaSBT (version 0.1.5)46 under the MIT license and installable as a Python 3.9 package from PyPI (pip install metasbt) and Bioconda47 (conda install -c bioconda metasbt). Software documentation is available through the GitHub Wiki on the same repository. The MetaSBT Data Model is also defined in the same GitHub repository.
Custom scripts and code used to reproduce the experiments presented in this study, including the inflammatory bowel disease analysis, the scalability benchmarks and the comparative tests, have been deposited at Zenodo and are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19900807 (ref. 48).
Finally, the tool suite for the Galaxy platform32 is available on the official Galaxy ToolShed49 after being reviewed and approved by the Intergalactic Utilities Commission, and it is fully integrated into the main instance of Galaxy (https://usegalaxy.org/) and the Galaxy Microbiology Lab50 instance (https://microbiology.usegalaxy.eu/). A comprehensive tutorial detailing how to use the MetaSBT tool suite in Galaxy is also available on the Galaxy Training Network51 at https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/microbiome/tutorials/metasbt/tutorial.html.
